title: Remark
body_md: The degree of the square free polynomial $f_{\mathrm{sf}}(x)$ is exactly the number of distinct roots of $f_U(x)$. If $U$ is periodic with the period $n$, then the number of distinct roots of $f_U(x)$ is at most $n$. Therefore $deg(f_{sf}) \leq n$.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: The splitting field of the original polynomial and the splitting field of its square-free part are the same, $L(f_U)=L(f_{\mathrm{sf}}).$
head: environment

label: lem:ramification of primes
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:ramification of primes}
   If \(p\) ramifies in \(L/\mathbb{Q}\), then \\ (a) either \(p\) ramifies in
\(K/\mathbb{Q}\), or \\ (b) there exists a prime ideal
\(\mathfrak{p}\subseteq\mathcal{O}_K\) lying above \(p\) that ramifies
in \(L/K\).
head: environment

label: lem:ramification-discriminant-cleared
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:ramification-discriminant-cleared} 
    If $\mathfrak{p}$ is a prime ideal of $\mathcal{O}_K$ lying above \(p\) that ramifies
in \(L\), then                                            
 $p$ divides $N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(Disc(f_{\mathrm{sf}}(x))$ or $c$.

label: thm:prime-divisors-of-cyclotomic-order
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:prime-divisors-of-cyclotomic-order}
Suppose \(U\) is a periodic unitary matrix with period \(n\) whose entries lie in a number field \(K\). Then, for every odd rational prime $p$ dividing $n$ , divides $\operatorname{Disc}(K/\mathbb{Q})$, or $c$, or $N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}\!\left(\operatorname{Disc}(F_{sf})\right)$.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
When $n\equiv2\pmod4$, the prime $2$ divides $n$ but is
unramified in $\mathbb Q(\zeta_n)$. We therefore include 2 by default in the set of all possible prime divisors of $n$ among the ones determined in Theorem \ref{thm:prime-divisors-of-cyclotomic-order}.

title: Remark
body_md: We emphasize that \(E\) need not itself satisfy $\varphi(E)\mid  [K:\mathbb{Q}]\,d_{\mathrm{sf}}!.$ The integer \(E\) is not being proposed as a candidate for the minimal period.

name: Ideals in \(\mathbb{Z}\

title: Example
body_md:
For
\[
K=\mathbb{Q}(i), \qquad \mathcal{O}_K=\mathbb{Z}[i],
\]
consider the principal ideal
\begin{equation}
    \mathfrak p = (1+i) = \left\{ (1+i)(a+bi): a,b\in\mathbb{Z} \right\}.
\end{equation}
This is a prime ideal because
\begin{equation}
    \mathbb{Z}[i]/(1+i)
    \cong
    \mathbb{F}_2,
\end{equation}
which is a field. Moreover,
\begin{equation}
    (2)
    =
    (1+i)^2
    =
    \mathfrak p^2,
\end{equation}
where multiplication by a unit does not change a principal ideal. The
contraction of \(\mathfrak p\) to \(\mathbb{Z}\) is
\begin{equation}
    \mathfrak p\cap\mathbb{Z}
    =
    (2).
\end{equation}
Thus, \(\mathfrak p=(1+i)\) is a prime ideal of \(\mathbb{Z}[i]\) lying
above the rational prime \(2\).

title: Proof
body_md:
Consider the tower $\mathbb{Q}\subseteq K\subseteq L.$ Choose a prime ideal $\mathfrak{P}\subseteq\mathcal{O}_L$ lying above \(p\) such that $e(\mathfrak{P}/p)>1.$
Define $\mathfrak{p} = \mathfrak{P}\cap\mathcal{O}_K.$

Then \(\mathfrak{p}\) is a prime ideal of \(\mathcal{O}_K\) lying above $p$. Hence, $\mathfrak{p}\cap\mathbb{Z}=(p).$ By the multiplicativity of ramification indices in a tower,
\[
e(\mathfrak{P}/p) = e(\mathfrak{P}/\mathfrak{p})\, e(\mathfrak{p}/p).
\]
Since $e(\mathfrak{P}/p)>1,$ at least one of the following two cases must occur.

\medskip

\noindent\textbf{Case A: $e(\mathfrak{p}/p)>1.$}

In this case, \(p\) is ramified in $K/\mathbb{Q}.$ 

\medskip

\noindent\textbf{Case B: $e(\mathfrak{P}/\mathfrak{p})>1.$}

In this case, the prime ideal \(\mathfrak{p}\) ramifies in $L/K.$
Equivalently, if
\[
\mathfrak{p}\mathcal{O}_L = \mathfrak{P}_1^{e_1} \mathfrak{P}_2^{e_2} \cdots \mathfrak{P}_g^{e_g},
\]
then $e_j>1$ for at least one \(j\).

\medskip

\noindent
\fbox{ 
\parbox{0.92\linewidth}{ 
If \(p\) ramifies in \(L/\mathbb{Q}\), then either \(p\) ramifies in
\(K/\mathbb{Q}\), or there exists a prime ideal
\(\mathfrak{p}\subseteq\mathcal{O}_K\) lying above \(p\) that ramifies
in \(L/K\).
}}

title: Proof
body_md:
By the defining property of the minimal polynomial, for every polynomial
\(q(x)\in K[x]\), \[ q(U)=0 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f_{\mathrm{sf}}(x)\mid q(x). \]
Applying this result to $ q(x)=x^k-\tau$ gives
\begin{align}
    U^k=\tau I
    &\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
    U^k-\tau I=0
    \nonumber\\
    &\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
    f_{\mathrm{sf}}(x)\mid x^k-\tau.
\end{align}

By the polynomial division algorithm, there exists a polynomial
\(a_k(x)\in K[x]\) such that
\[
x^k=a_k(x)f_{\mathrm{sf}}(x)+\rho_k(x), \qquad \deg\rho_k<d_{\mathrm{sf}}. 
\]
The divisibility condition
\[
f_{\mathrm{sf}}(x)\mid x^k-\tau
\]
holds if and only if the remainder of \(x^k-\tau\) upon division by
\(f_{\mathrm{sf}}(x)\) is zero. Since this remainder is $\rho_k(x)-\tau,$
the divisibility condition is equivalent to $\rho_k(x)=\tau.$
Therefore,
\[
U^k=\tau I \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \rho_k(x)=\tau,
\]
as claimed.
